Title: Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids

Abstract: Membrane capacity during the filtration of biotech process streams is typically limited by fouling, which can occur by pore blocking, pore constriction, caking or a combination of the mechanisms. In this study five new fouling models that accounted for the combined effects of the different individual fouling mechanisms were generated. Explicit equations were derived from Darcy's law that related pressure to time during constant flow operation and volume to time during constant pressure operation. The models used two fitted parameters and reduced to the individual models when one mechanism dominated. The applicability of the models to data for the sterile filtration of IgG and the viral filtration of BSA was tested. The combined caking and complete blockage model was the most useful, as it was able to provide good fits of both data sets, and provide good fits of each of the other individual model predictions. The cake-complete model will provide good fits of a broad range of curves where the flux declines in a manner between the extremes of cake filtration and complete blocking. The combined cake-standard and cake-intermediate models also provided good data fits and may be applicable to systems where these models are consistent with the experimentally observed fouling mechanisms.

Model: Cake-standard blocking
Laws:
(1) [constitutive] Darcy's law computes the filtration flow rate from trans-membrane pressure, membrane area, resistance, and solution viscosity.
(2) [constitutive] The standard-blocking model computes filtration resistance as a function of permeate volume processed per membrane area.
(11) [constitutive] The cake-filtration model computes total resistance relative to initial resistance as a function of permeate volume.
(14) [constitutive] The Darcy relation computes normalized flux from the change in filtration resistance and available membrane area under constant pressure.
(20) [constitutive] The constant-pressure Darcy relation computes normalized flux from the change in filtration resistance.
(21) [constitutive] The combined standard-blocking and cake-filtration law computes normalized flux as a function of processed volume.
(24) [constitutive] At constant flow, pressure relative to its reference value scales with filtration resistance and inversely with available membrane area.
(29) [constitutive] The combined cake-standard-blocking model computes pressure over time as resistance increases while membrane area remains constant.

States (computed by the ODEs):


Inputs (variables no law computes):
- A: available membrane frontal area
- V: permeate volume processed per membrane area
- J_{0}: initial flux
- P_{0}: initial reference pressure
- t: time

Model-wide assumptions:
- Standard blocking assumes that particles accumulate inside membranes on the walls of straight cylindrical pores.
- Deposited aggregates are permeable.

answer.description: The model describes fouling during membrane filtration of biological fluids, with applications to sterile filtration of IgG and viral filtration of BSA. It predicts filtration flux or pressure as filtration proceeds under constant-pressure or constant-flow operation. Darcy's law is combined with standard-blocking and cake-filtration laws; standard blocking assumes particles accumulate on pore walls, while deposited aggregates form a permeable cake.
